name: Felix Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a three-person studio on the market square, above the chemist. We do a bit of everything for the town: shop signs, the football club's kit sponsor logos, banners for the farm show, the church newsletter, and sadly a lot of funeral programmes. Today it's the agricultural show banner, which has to be readable from across a muddy field. My boss Gordon has run the place for thirty years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the people I design for. When the butcher's new sign went up, half the street came out to look. What wears me out is the pay, which isn't great, and the fact that I'm getting married next September to Anna. We've got less than a month of savings and a wedding to pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people can get back to proper work. I'd say it at the pub after the football. I've never used the AI things and I wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm worried anyway. The wedding is going to cost more than we've got, and my pay hasn't gone up in two years. Gordon is near retirement and nobody knows what happens to the studio after him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my work and ask Gordon straight out what his plans are. I'd pick up extra hours at my uncle Viktor's sign and van-wrap shop on Saturdays. Anna and I would cut the wedding guest list from a hundred and twenty to about eighty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about computers, about money and the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the wedding would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band goes first. Anna's mum won't like it, but a playlist is fine. The church service and the hall at the cricket club stay in the wedding, because they're the bits that matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Gordon said he was selling up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask if I could buy into it, though I've no money. More likely I'd go to Viktor full time. Family looks after family, that's how we were raised.

say: I'd say good, people can get back to **proper work**.
I'd say I've never used the **AI things** and won't start.
think: I'm worried about the **wedding costs** and two years without a raise.
Gordon (my boss) is near **retirement**, and nobody knows what follows.
do: Ask Gordon **straight out** about his plans.
Work **Saturdays** at Uncle Viktor's sign and van-wrap shop.
Cut the wedding list from **120 to 80**.
feel: **Anxious** about **money** and the wedding, not computers.
S0.quote: The church service and the hall at the cricket club stay in the wedding, because they're the bits that matter.
fieldNote: Felix's worries come from the **wedding** and an ageing boss, not AI.
He leans on **family** first, through his uncle's sign shop.
He holds firmly to what **matters** to him: church and community.

steps.text: Ask Gordon directly what happens to the studio after he retires
Work Saturdays at Uncle Viktor's sign and van-wrap shop
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80 and drop the band

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but businesses will do what's cheapest, that's how it works. I'd say people should support local firms who use real people. I'd put that on the studio's page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the studio's in real trouble. Gordon might just close rather than learn new software at sixty-two. And I'm no help there, because I don't use it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Viktor if he could take me on properly, cutting vinyl and fitting signs and van wraps. That's hands-on, you're up a ladder or on your knees by a van. Anna and I would push the wedding back a year and save for it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I've missed a train everyone else saw coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the tools, to keep the studio going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not good with new software, and I don't trust it. Gordon's the same. I'd rather work with my hands for family than sit at a screen doing what a machine tells me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Anna feel about pushing the wedding back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disappointed, but she's practical. Her dad would say the same thing, don't start married life in debt. We'd still get engaged at church as planned, just marry later.

feel: **Anxious**, like he's **missed a train** others saw coming.
S1.quote: I'd rather work with my hands for family than sit at a screen doing what a machine tells me.
fieldNote: Felix accepts **market logic** but wants people to buy local.
He expects his **ageing boss** to close rather than adapt.

steps.text: Ask Uncle Viktor for a full-time job fitting signs and van wraps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's gone too fast and people need to stick together, families, churches, neighbours. I don't want handouts, I want work. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the studio's gone within a year, and my design training with it. That's all screen work. The only reason I'd sleep at all is Viktor's shop, which is hands-on and should last until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Viktor's full time the first month. Anna and I would marry small, just family at the church, no hall, no party. We'd look at moving into the flat above Viktor's workshop to cut the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground went from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come around 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Van wraps are fiddly, bubbles and curves, but I suppose a robot learns. I'd be thirty-two with a wife and no plan. That's the part I can't think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there were no work at all, I'd take it, but I'd hate it. I'd rather do any job going, stacking shelves, anything. My grandfather never took a penny he didn't earn.

say: I'd say people need to stick together: **families, churches**, neighbours.
I'd say I want **work**, not handouts, and I'd say it to anyone.
think: The studio's gone within **a year**, with my design training.
Viktor's **hands-on** shop should last until about 2031.

Move into the flat above Viktor's **workshop**.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if the **ground** went from under him.
S2.quote: Van wraps are fiddly, bubbles and curves, but I suppose a robot learns. I'd be thirty-two with a wife and no plan.
fieldNote: Felix's family business is a real **lifeline** that buys about three years.
He would accept **state help** only as a last resort, and resents it.

steps.text: Join Uncle Viktor's sign and van-wrap shop full time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families and firms to sort themselves out, without the government making a mess of it. Apprenticeships, not courses. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at the studio a couple more years and then go to Viktor's. The design side goes in 2031, the van wraps maybe 2034. That's enough to get married and settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd ask Viktor to start teaching me wrapping on Saturdays, properly, like an apprentice. We'd keep the wedding date but cut it down to about eighty people. I'd put fifty a week aside from the Saturday money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I can see a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships, not courses. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you learn from someone who's done it for years, in the real place. Courses give you a certificate and no customers. My uncle Viktor learned from his father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the lads at football?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade with your hands, while you've got time. Most of them work in offices or warehouses. I'd say it, but I don't think they'd listen until it's too late.

say: I'd say firms and families should sort it out without **government** making a mess.
think: I'd stay at the studio **two more years**, then go to Viktor's.
Design goes in **2031**, van wraps maybe 2034.

S3.quote: Courses give you a certificate and no customers. My uncle Viktor learned from his father.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot gap** as time to get married and settled.

steps.text: Learn van wrapping on Saturdays as Uncle Viktor's apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should be crying for help. Work hard, learn a trade, look after your own. I'd say it with a clear conscience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I could stay a designer for most of it. I'd keep the studio going with Gordon, maybe take it over. But I'd still want the sign shop as a back door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd marry Anna as planned, the full wedding. I'd ask Gordon about taking over the studio when he retires, paying him over time. And I'd help Viktor on Saturdays, just to keep my hand in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit, but much less. It's the kind of worry you can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Taking over a studio in a world where design is going. Is that wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. Taking over the studio would be mine, and I'd sell signs and printing with it, not just designs. If it fails, I'll have learned to run a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want them, two or three, soon after the wedding. I'd want to own something by then. Family's the point of all this.

I'd still want the **sign shop** as a back door.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be newly married with no work and no savings. What would help is proper apprenticeships, with firms paid a bit to take people on, so young men like me can learn a trade from someone who knows it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the town. When the studio and the printer and the shops all go to machines, who's left on the market square? That's what I'd miss.

headlineQuote: When the studio and the printer and the shops all go to machines, who's left on the market square?
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old designer** at a three-person studio on a **market square**.
He's engaged to Anna, and the **wedding** shapes most of his money decisions.
He never uses AI, accepts market logic, and leans on **family** rather than the state.
His escape route in every picture is his uncle Viktor's **sign shop**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, newly married with no work and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **apprenticeships**, with firms paid a little to take people on.
